turns.prompt_text: I'd like to build some kind of computer visual system to be able to comvert my paper and whiteboard notes into svg images
turns.response_html:
Building a custom computer vision (CV) pipeline to turn whiteboard sketches and handwritten notes into clean, scalable SVG vector graphics is a great project. It sits right at the intersection of traditional image processing and modern vector generation.

To get clean SVGs, you essentially need a pipeline that handles image preprocessing, contour/path extraction, and vectorization.

Here is a high-level architectural blueprint of how you can build this system, using Python as the core language.

The System Architecture

[ Raw Image/Camera ] 
         │
         ▼
[ Preprocessing (OpenCV) ]  ───► Perspective correction, binarization, denoising
         │
         ▼
[ Feature Extraction ]      ───► Contour tracing, line thinning (skeletonization)
         │
         ▼
[ Vectorization Engine ]    ───► Potrace API or Bezier curve fitting
         │
         ▼
[ Clean SVG Output ]

Step 1: Document Layout & Preprocessing (OpenCV)

Paper and whiteboards introduce challenges like skewed angles, uneven lighting, and shadows. Your first module needs to clean the canvas.

  • Perspective Correction (The "CamScanner" Effect): Find the four corners of the paper or whiteboard frame using contour detection (cv2.findContours) and apply a perspective warp (cv2.getPerspectiveTransform) to flatten the image into a top-down view.
  • Binarization (Adaptive Thresholding): Standard thresholding fails with shadows. Use adaptive thresholding (cv2.adaptiveThreshold) or Otsu's binarization to separate the ink cleanly from the background, turning it into a crisp black-and-white mask.
  • Morphological Operations: Use dilation and erosion (cv2.morphologyEx) to close minor gaps in your pen strokes and remove isolated speckles of noise.

Step 2: Feature Extraction & Skeletonization

Depending on what kind of notes you are converting, you have two primary paths for vectorization:

Path A: Solid Shapes and Thick Lettering (Contour Tracking)

If your notes contain solid shapes, diagrams, or thick markers, you want to track the outer boundary of the ink. OpenCV’s contour retrieval finds these boundaries perfectly.

Path B: Line Drawings and Mathematical Formulas (Skeletonization)

If you want your SVG to consist of single-stroke lines (like a true pen path) rather than outline shapes, you need to "thin" the detected lines until they are exactly 1 pixel wide.

  • You can use the Zhang-Suen skeletonization algorithm (available via skimage.morphology.skeletonize) to reduce strokes to their central skeletons.

Step 3: The Vectorization Engine (Raster to Vector)

Once you have a clean, binarized bitmap or skeleton, you need to translate pixels into SVG paths ($P_0 \rightarrow P_1$ control points).

Option 1: The Potrace Route (Fastest & Most Reliable)

Potrace is the industry standard open-source tool for transforming bitmaps into vectors (it powers Inkscape's vectorization).

  • How to implement: Use the Python binding pypotrace or invoke the potrace CLI directly from your script using subprocess.
  • Input: Your processed black-and-white OpenCV image.
  • Output: A native, scalable SVG file.

Option 2: Custom Bezier Curve Fitting (The DIY Math Route)

If you want to build the vectorizer from scratch without external binaries, you can parse the pixel coordinates of your paths and fit mathematical curves to them.

  • Algorithm: Use Schneider’s Curve Fitting Algorithm to convert an array of sequential pixel coordinates into a series of cubic Bezier curves.
  • Implementation: Loop through your detected contours, apply the curve-fitting function to smooth the jittery pixel edges, and format the output strings into standard SVG <path d="..." /> syntax.

Recommended Tech Stack

ComponentLibrary / ToolPurpose
Image ProcessingOpenCV (opencv-python)Thresholding, perspective warps, and contour detection.
Advanced Thinningscikit-imageHigh-quality skeletonization for single-stroke line notes.
Vector Corepypotrace or potrace CLITranslating the cleaned binary array into vector paths.
File HandlingsvgwriteA clean Python library to structure, layer, and save the final SVG XML.

Next Steps to Start Coding

  1. Prototype the pipeline in a Jupyter Notebook: Start by feeding it a static, well-lit photo of a whiteboard diagram.
  2. Fine-tune the thresholding: Whiteboards often have glare. Experiment with bilateral filtering (cv2.bilateralFilter) before thresholding to smooth out lighting gradients while preserving sharp pen edges.
  3. Automation: Once the core pipeline works, you can wrap it in a lightweight CLI tool, or even trigger it automatically whenever a new image hits a specific file directory.

Are you leaning more toward preserving the "outline" thickness of your marker drawings, or do you want to resolve everything down to single-stroke mathematical vectors?
